title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 17: Achieving Judicial Goals the Rotary Way
keywords: Achieving Judicial Goals the Rotary Way
those with less in life should have more in law
primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's first major policy address before a private organization, delivered to the Rotary Club of Manila forty-two days into his chief justiceship, laying out his whole program as the 21st Chief Justice.

The Rotary origin of his public career: it was through his Rotary presidency in 1990-1991 that then President-elect Fidel V. Ramos came to know him, offered him the justice portfolio he declined, and eventually appointed him to the Supreme Court in 1995.

His judicial philosophy stated as two standards of judicial review -- in cases involving civil liberties the scales weigh heavily in favor of the people, especially the poor and marginalized, while in conflicts affecting prosperity and development deference is due the Presidency and Congress -- serving the twin objectives of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

The answer to 'too much to do, too little time': Rotary, whose presidents serve only twelve months yet are remembered for great deeds, is his model, and he backs it with what he had already done in 42 days -- the JDF advisory committee, the strategic planning workshop, the PhilJA grant, Justice on Wheels, e-payment and the Sandiganbayan's computerization.
sub_topics: Why the Rotary Club of Manila was chosen as the venue: Rotary 'had initiated me into the government.'

The June 17, 1992 offer from President-elect Fidel V. Ramos of the justice secretaryship, which CJP declined on the ground that he had not campaigned for Ramos and that Cabinet members should come from the President's political circle.

Ramos's reply that noninvolvement in the campaign was immaterial, that he had observed CJP closely during his 1990-1991 Rotary presidency, and that he recalled their private conversations about the role of law in good government.

The eventual offer of an associate justiceship, 'an offer I could not resist,' and CJP's acknowledgment that without Rotary and the 1995 appointment he might never have become Chief Justice -- with the note that Ramos never asked him a single favor and absolutely respected his independence.

The pledge to lead a judiciary of four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- morally courageous against influence, interference, insolence and indifference, and closed to the plague of 'ships': kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship.

The parallel vision for the bar -- the 'vineyard from which our judges are picked' -- of lawyers giving quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal service as CJ Davide required, owing utmost fidelity to truth and justice above their clients' causes, and serving as beacons for the weak, the oppressed and the disadvantaged.
The loftier objectives on which he stakes his chief justiceship: safeguarding the people's liberty and nurturing their prosperity while upholding the rule of law and judicial independence.
The two standards of judicial policy in exercising judicial review, stated as a pair and then explained in turn.

Protecting liberty: the 1987 Constitution springing from the struggle for human dignity, the Bill of Rights' detailed guarantee that individual liberties must be fully safeguarded against the enormous powers of the State, the courts' duty to protect the weak and defenseless, Magsaysay's line that those with less in life should have more in law, and the Court's quasi-legislative power to promulgate rules on the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights.

Deference on economic and policy questions, with the balancing formulation quoted from his 2004 book 'Leveling the Playing Field' and the rule that in case of doubt the Court upholds the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts.
The short-term agenda for 2006: continuing CJ Davide's reform program and the APJR while focusing on the ACID problems of access, corruption, incompetence and delay.

The objection he voices on his critics' behalf -- can a Chief Justice accomplish a grand vision in barely one year? -- and the Rotary answer that a twelve-month presidency can still be remembered for great deeds.

His preparation: seven years as a Rotary member before his 1990-1991 presidency, when he was inducted with a ready theme, 'Love God, Serve Man,' and a month-by-month, week-by-week program; and ten years on the Supreme Court before his elevation, resolving cases speedily, working long hours, writing one book a year, and heading reform committees.

First accomplishment -- a press conference the day after his oath spelling out the 'Liberty and Prosperity' philosophy, the four Ins and the fight against ACID, followed by a no-holds-barred one-hour interview with Korina Sanchez televised on ANC.

Second -- a transparency measure: an advisory committee on the Judiciary Development Fund, whose controversy nearly caused CJ Davide's impeachment in 2003, including the heads of judges' associations and employee organizations; plus the disbursement of all available 2005 JDF funds and savings in three January tranches to some 28,000 judiciary employees.

Third -- an all-day Strategic Planning Workshop on January 12, 2006 with over 100 top magistrates and officials, producing a detailed 2006 strategic plan with activities, targets, milestones, responsible offices and timelines.

Concrete results in 42 days: the January 18, 2006 turnover by Japanese Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki of a P300 million grant for the PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay, envisioned as an ASEAN center for judicial excellence and an answer to incompetence.

The activation on January 30, 2006 of the second and third 'Justice on Wheels' mobile courts, following the December 19, 2004 pilot, bringing bus-borne courts to far-flung areas without courtrooms and serving the access component of ACID.

The pilot e-payment system for remitting docket and court fees directly to the banking system, replacing manual collection by clerks of court some of whom had 'borrowed' from or delayed remitting the fees -- addressing both corruption and delay in employees' benefits.

The March inauguration of the Sandiganbayan's full computerization, funded by USAID at minimal or no expense to the government and planned by the Supreme Court Computerization Committee he had long headed, as the model for the entire judiciary.

The peroration: one year is enough for a Rotarian, and his pledge, a thousand times more fervent than his Rotary vow of 'service above self,' that his 'RENAISSANCE COURT' of one year will be a model judiciary in the region.

stances.claim: In cases involving civil liberties the scales should weigh heavily in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak, because when pitted against the enormous powers of the State individual liberties must be fully safeguarded.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional grounding plus a borrowed maxim: the 1987 Constitution's origin in the struggle for human dignity, the Bill of Rights' detail, and Magsaysay's 'less in life, more in law' fused into a standard of review

stances.claim: In conflicts affecting prosperity and development, courts must defer to the Presidency and Congress, give reasonable leeway on economic policy, and in case of doubt uphold the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts.
stances.rhetorical_move: paired-standards symmetry: the deference rule stated as the deliberate counterweight to the liberty rule, backed by self-citation of 'Leveling the Playing Field'

stances.claim: A single year is enough to accomplish a grand judicial vision, because Rotary presidents serve only twelve months yet are remembered for great deeds, and because a decade of preparation preceded the office.

notable_anecdotes: CJP recounts that on June 17, 1992 President-elect Fidel V. Ramos offered him the justice secretaryship and that he declined, saying he was unworthy because he had not campaigned and that Cabinet members should come from the President's political circle -- only for Ramos to reply that his noninvolvement was immaterial.

Ramos told him he had observed him closely during his 1990-1991 Rotary presidency and repeatedly recalled their private conversations at Rotary meetings about the role of law in bringing about good government; the associate justiceship that followed was 'an offer I could not resist.'

He notes pointedly that President Ramos never asked him a favor for himself, his family, his political goals or even his administration, and absolutely respected his independence and integrity on the Court.

He recalls being inducted Rotary president in 1990 with a ready theme, 'Love God, Serve Man,' and a ready program complete with a month-by-month and week-by-week timetable -- the model he now applies to a one-year chief justiceship.

He describes giving a no-holds-barred, unprecedented one-hour interview to Korina Sanchez, televised several times on ANC, the day after his oath, to tell the public what to expect from the Panganiban Court.

He recalls that the Judiciary Development Fund controversy nearly caused CJ Davide's impeachment in 2003, which is why he created a JDF advisory committee including the heads of judges' associations and employee organizations.
He explains why the e-payment pilot matters by naming the practice it replaces: clerks of court who were tempted to 'borrow' from collected fees or to delay remitting them indefinitely.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's first major policy address before a private organization, given to the Rotary Club of Manila forty-two days after he assumed office on December 21, 2005. He explained that he chose Rotary because it had initiated him into government: on June 17, 1992 then President-elect Fidel V. Ramos, a Manila Rotarian, offered him the justice portfolio, which he declined for not having campaigned; Ramos answered that this was immaterial, having observed him closely during his 1990-1991 Rotary presidency, and later offered the associate justiceship he accepted in 1995 -- an appointment, he noted, for which Ramos never asked a favor. He pledged a judiciary of four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- morally courageous against influence, interference, insolence and indifference and closed to the plague of 'ships,' and a legal profession owing fidelity to truth and justice above clients' interests. His objectives were to safeguard the people's liberty and nurture their prosperity, pursued through two standards of judicial review: in civil-liberties cases the scales weigh heavily for the people, especially the poor and marginalized, invoking the Bill of Rights and Magsaysay's line that those with less in life should have more in law; in conflicts affecting prosperity and development, deference is owed the political departments, as he had argued in 'Leveling the Playing Field.' He committed to continuing Chief Justice Davide's reform program and to the ACID agenda. Answering the objection that this was too much for one year, he cited Rotary, whose presidents serve twelve months yet are remembered for great deeds, and his own decade of preparation on the Court. He then listed what he had done: a press conference and a televised interview with Korina Sanchez; a JDF advisory committee created for transparency after the 2003 controversy, plus disbursement of 2005 JDF funds to some 28,000 employees; an all-day Strategic Planning Workshop on January 12, 2006; and four concrete results -- the P300 million Japanese grant for the PhilJA Development Center, the second and third Justice on Wheels mobile courts, the e-payment pilot for court fees, and the USAID-funded computerization of the Sandiganbayan -- closing with a pledge that his 'RENAISSANCE COURT' of one year would be a model judiciary in the region.
